articles.title_orig: 2 Giant Pandas Arrive at Zoo Atlanta From China. Meet Ping Ping and Fu Shuang!
articles.title_zh: 2 Giant Pandas Arrive at Zoo Atlanta From China. Meet Ping Ping and Fu Shuang!
articles.content_orig:
Exclusive Deals on Stony Clover Lane, Ninja, Haus Labs and More
Two giant pandas arrived at Zoo Atlanta over the weekend, becoming the third zoo in the United States to house the animals as part of conservation agreements with China.
Ping Ping, 6, and Fu Shuang, 5, arrived early in the morning on Sept. 27 after a 16-hour flight aboard an aircraft known as the “FedEx Panda Express.” They will remain in the U.S. for 10 years.
The bears, who are not yet available for the public to see, will stay in a “biosecure area” of Zoo Atlanta to quarantine for about a month, the zoo said in a statement. The zoo will announce when and where visitors can view the pandas at a later date.
Zoo Atlanta President Raymond B. King called the pandas’ arrival a “historic moment.”
“Zoo Atlanta is honored to partner with the China Wildlife Conservation Association to see important work continue toward the conservation of giant pandas, which is the most important benefit of guarding this species,” King added.
The animals traveled on a private plane with custom crates and plenty of fresh bamboo, water and treats. After touching down in Atlanta, they received a police escort to Zoo Atlanta.
Ping Ping, who is a boy, is described as plump with a love of food. Fu Shuang, a girl, is smart and playful with a zest for apples.
In May, NBC’s Janis Mackey Frayer was able to visit Fu Shuang and Ping Ping before they made the nearly 8,000-mile flight.
Ping Ping’s keepers said he tends to follow them around, which is atypical behavior for a panda but may be because of the food they have for him. Fu Shuang — which translates to “double happiness” — is playful but nervous, and she enjoys placing her chin on her paw.
“Because we will hide pieces of apples, for example under the tree ... she can find them everywhere,” panda keeper Wang Shun told Mackey Frayer, noting her “clever” behavior.
Chinese President Xi Jinping called the pandas’ move to Atlanta “an envoy of friendship” while he was at the White House last week.
The pandas are part of an international cooperative research agreement on giant panda conservation between Zoo Atlanta and the China Wildlife Conservation Association, the latest example of panda diplomacy between America and China, which began in 1972.
Pandas are already at zoos in Washington, D.C. , and San Diego . Zoo Atlanta maintained a panda agreemen t with China from 1999 until 2024, when giant pandas Lun Lun and Yang Yang went back to their home country, along with their two youngest cubs.
Drew Weisholtz is a reporter for TODAY Digital, focusing on pop culture, nostalgia and trending stories. He has seen every episode of “Saved by the Bell” at least 50 times, longs to perfect the crane kick from “The Karate Kid” and performs stand-up comedy, while also cheering on the New York Yankees and New York Giants. A graduate of Rutgers University, he is the married father of two kids who believe he is ridiculous.

articles.title_orig: Opinion | China is no longer just the world’s factory. It’s the HQ
articles.title_zh: Opinion | China is no longer just the world’s factory. It’s the HQ
articles.content_orig:
Manufacturing capacity is moving overseas but China, as a global hub for innovation and development, remains the ‘industrial brain’
The global electronics industry is entering a structural transition. For over two decades, China served as the dominant manufacturing centre, with an unmatched concentration of suppliers, skilled labour, infrastructure, logistics and engineering capabilities. That concentration is being diluted. But interpreting this as the decline of Chinese manufacturing would be a mistake.
According to the Boston Consulting Group (BCG), since 2017, the share of electronics manufacturers from China – Taiwan, Hong Kong and the mainland – with overseas production has risen to 56 per cent from 12 per cent. BCG based its analysis on 942 publicly traded companies with annual revenues above US$500 million, including 314 headquartered in China. This transformation is remarkable.

Gold and silver prices slipped sharply on Monday, as rising global bond yields cooled investor appetite for non-interest-bearing assets, like precious metals. The sell-off also dragged major mining stocks lower in premarket trading.
Gold futures slumped 3.34% to $4,176.80, while spot gold prices were off by 3.27% at $4,145.88 around 5:40 a.m. E.T.
Silver, meanwhile, fell even further. Silver futures were last seen 5.1% lower at $61.52 per troy ounce, while spot silver had shed 4.92% to $61.11.
U.S.-listed shares of global gold and silver miners dropped in premarket trading on the back of the retreat.
Sibanye Stillwater , a major gold producer which is also active in platinum and palladium markets, was 7.92% lower ahead of Monday's market open, while Harmony Gold Mining slumped 7.49%. Newmont Corporation was down 4.72% in premarket trading.
Among silver miners, Silvercorp Metals was down 7.13%, Endeavour Silver shed 5.86%, and Hecla Mining dipped 5.55%.
The downward moves come as investors continue to monitor inflationary pressures and the likelihood of further interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve against a backdrop of surging government bond yields .
"If hikes bring inflation under control, gold faces sustained pressure," Max Baecker, president of American Hartford Gold, said in a note Friday. "If inflation sticks or economic stress builds, demand for gold as a diversifier holds."
Baecker added that rates are "just one piece of the gold story," noting how global central banks purchased a record 289 metric tons in the second quarter, which he sees as a longer-term reserve strategy separate from Fed rate decisions.

Fox News' Lucas Tomlinson reports the latest on the threat from Iranian hackers targeting U.S. infrastructure.
U.K. police say they arrested multiple suspects for offenses under the "Explosives Act" near a U.S. airbase in southwest England on Sunday.
Gloucestershire Police say the arrests took place just two miles from RAF Fairford, which hosts U.S. Air Force assets. The U.S. has recently used the base in operations relating to the war in Iran.
"A number of properties are currently being evacuated in the Whelford area following the declaration of a major incident," Gloucestershire Police said in a statement. "It follows the arrest of several men on suspicion of offenses under the explosives act."
ANDY BURNHAM TAKES OVER AS UK PRIME MINISTER, CALLS FOR 'NEW POLITICAL MODEL'
Police at a road block on the road to RAF Fairford after a major incident has been declared, with armed police manning a cordon near the village of Whelford in Gloucestershire, near RAF Fairford which is used by the United States Air Force (USAF). Picture date: Sunday, September 27, 2026. (Photo by Ben Birchall/PA Images via Getty Images)
"The Army's specialist explosive ordnance disposal team are currently examining a number of vehicles," police added.
President Donald Trump responded to news of the arrests while talking to the press later Sunday.
"The arrest in the UK was fantastic. Working with Britain. It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation," Trump said of the suspects. "They, they were looking to do big damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great."
A reporter then asked if the suspects were migrants, and Trump demurred.
"It may have been Scotland Yard. I don't know that we worked with a lot of them. We had them under review for a long time and we got them," Trump said.
Authorities did not name the suspects or detail exactly how many were arrested.
British Defense Secretary Wes Streeting wrote on X that the situation is "being dealt with."
UK PINS STRING OF ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS ON IRAN-LINKED GROUP, BANS IRGC
A B1 Bomber at RAF Fairford on July 25, 2026, in Fairford, England. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has declared RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire a "legitimate target" after U.S. Air Force B-1B Lancer bombers used the British base to launch defensive bombing missions against Iranian military targets. (Photo by Matthew Horwood/Getty Images)
Prime Minister Andy Burnham also released a statement on the arrests.
"I know today's incident near RAF Fairford will be deeply concerning for local residents and for many people following developments across the country. My thanks go to Gloucestershire Police, Counter Terrorism Policing, our Armed Forces and all those working to keep the public safe," he said.
"The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe. The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts," he added.
WATER CYBERATTACK HITS AT LEAST 7 STATES
The incident comes roughly a month after Iran-linked hackers were suspected of forcing a small British power generator offline for several days this summer.
The British shutdown came weeks after hackers struck more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota , accessing technology used to remotely monitor and control pumps and other equipment. Minnesota officials have not publicly attributed the attacks. Several news outlets, citing U.S. officials and a leaked industry threat-sharing memo, reported that Iran was the likely culprit.

articles.title_orig: Sources: Giants' Brian Burns believed to have torn ACL
articles.title_zh: Sources: Giants' Brian Burns believed to have torn ACL
articles.content_orig:
The Giants likely have now lost their most important offensive player and their best defensive player to season-ending injuries in back-to-back weeks.
Star pass rusher Brian Burns is feared to have suffered a torn ACL during Sunday’s 12-7 win over the Titans, according to ESPN .
Burns, who played Sunday despite suffering an ankle sprain in Week 2, went down early in the fourth quarter and did not return to the game.
“There is some hope there,” Giants head coach John Harbaugh said after improving to 2-1, “but we won’t know until we see the MRI.”
This crushing injury comes one week after the Giants lost quarterback Jaxson Dart for the season after suffering damage to his left knee, including his MCL and PCL .
Losing Burns is a massive blow to a Giants pass rush that has underwhelmed to start the season.
Burns ranked second in the NFL last season with 16.5 sacks, although he had yet to take down the quarterback this season.
The Giants rank 31st with their one sack, ahead of only the winless Dolphins, who are generally believed to be the worst team in the NFL.
Burns, 28, is in the third season of a five-year, $141 million extension he signed after being acquired by the team in 2024 and has been a standout during these lean years.
He has yet to miss a game since joining the franchise and has 25 sacks in 37 games.
With Burns set to miss the season, pending free agent Kayvon Thibodeaux will take on a greater role opposite second-year edge rusher Abdul Carter.
Carter has the Giants’ lone sack, tallied during the 28-6 loss to the Rams in Week 2.
The Giants host the Cardinals (2-1) on Sunday in what is a winnable game, but being without Dart and now Burns for final 14 contests provides quite an uphill challenge for Harbaugh and Co.
More to come on this developing story…

British counterterrorism police are leading an investigation after five men were arrested on suspicion of explosives offenses and preparing a terrorist act near an air base used by U.S. forces.
Police received a report at around 12:45 a.m. Sunday about three suspicious vehicles traveling toward RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, southwestern England. Armed officers responded and arrested the men in nearby Whelford.
Fairford is used as a forward operating location for the U.S. Air Force Global Strike Command. The base has hosted U.S. B-52 and B-1 bombers during the Iran war , according to ABC News . American forces have used Fairford to carry out strikes against Iranian missile sites, the Associated Press reported.
Read More: Why More Republicans Are Breaking With Trump on Iran
In a press conference Sunday, Assistant Chief Constable Richard Ocone said that about 85 households in the area were advised to evacuate early Sunday morning as a precaution.
"A 400m cordon has been put in place around the vehicles, while the Army's Explosive Ordnance Disposal Unit examine them,” Ocone said. A statement from police earlier Sunday said that they believe the situation is “contained.”
Aerial footage from Sky News shows a bomb disposal robot moving between three white vans at the site, with the rear doors of two vehicles open.
Ocone added that the men remain in custody and will be questioned by police.
The base is home to both the 501st Combat Support Wing Headquarters and the 420th Air Base Squadron, and serves as the “preferred bomber forward operating location in Europe,” according to the U.S. Air Force.
TIME has reached out to the U.S. Air Force for comment on the incident.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who assumed the post in July, called the incident “deeply concerning” on X .
“The safety and security of the public is our first priority, and I want people to know that we will always take every step necessary to protect our communities and keep our country safe,” he wrote. “The investigation remains ongoing, and I would urge people not to speculate while the authorities establish the full facts.” When asked by reporters about the arrests, U.S. President Donald Trump called them “fantastic.” “They were looking to do big damage to our fort,” Trump said of the suspects, “and working with the British worked out great.”
Trump also said the suspects had been under surveillance before their arrests. “We had them under view for a long time, and we got them,” he said.
British police have not confirmed that RAF Fairford was the intended target of the suspected attacks. The Associated Press reported that investigators were considering a possible connection to Iran, but no such link has been confirmed.

articles.title_orig: US and China agree to cut tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods, from coal to toys
articles.title_zh: US and China agree to cut tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods, from coal to toys
articles.content_orig:
The United States and China have agreed to slash tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods, deepening efforts to stabilize a frequently testy relationship.
The tariff relief extends to an array of products, from US coal and agricultural products to made-in-China toys, car seats and holiday decorations.
The announcement from the White House late Sunday followed a highly anticipated meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington last week.
The White House said that under a so-called “30-for-30” framework, each country would be allowed to import “non-sensitive” goods worth $30 billion from the other at reduced tariff rates.
The more favorable tariff treatment followed recommendations from the US-China Board of Trade and would improve market access for about 30% of US exports to China, US trade representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement Sunday.
The Trump-Xi meeting was heavy on pomp, light on substance. China is just fine with that
“The Trump Administration will continue to pursue fair, balanced, and reciprocal trade with China by ensuring compliance with commitments on agricultural and energy purchases, pursuing balanced trade in non-sensitive goods, and securing market access for American farmers, manufacturers, businesses, and workers,” he added.
The Chinese list of US products that will be subject to lower tariffs covers 1,619 items, including corn, wheat, frozen meat, seafood, wood products, cosmetics and medical devices, according to a list published by the White House . US soybeans were not included, a blow to struggling American farmers who have been collateral damage from a years-long tit-for-tat trade war between the two countries.
The White House also said that China would import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the United States in 2027 and again in 2028. Previous commitments to import certain quantities of goods, such as agricultural products, have not always been met in full, however.
The US list of Chinese imports covers 77 items, including toys, tableware, kitchen accessories, curtains, electric shavers and inflatable balls.
The Chinese commerce ministry said the agreement would “further stabilize” China-US economic and trade relations and “create favorable conditions” for the export of relevant Chinese products to the United States.
The announcement comes after the US and China agreed ahead of Xi’s visit to press pause on escalating tariff measures until January 10. The trade truce – which sets tariff levels at 30% on Chinese goods and 10% on US goods – has been extended multiple times since May 2025, when the two countries met in Geneva for negotiations.
The goods listed Sunday, however, will likely be carved out of future tariff measures.
Trump has used tariffs to narrow the US trade deficit with China – or the difference between what America exports to China and what it imports from China – prompting Chinese exporters to send more goods elsewhere, including to Europe.
In an interview with CNBC on Friday, Greer said the deficit on goods trade with China had fallen 40% since Trump took office and was on track to reach $140 billion this year. Data from the US Census Bureau showed the deficit amounted to around $295 billion in 2024.
Beyond trade, the two countries also agreed to establish a bilateral communication channel to discuss any artificial intelligence-related “incidents,” according to the White House.
The White House said Xi and Trump agreed to use the term “super intelligence” rather than “artificial intelligence” to describe the emerging technology, and that the two sides had established the. U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue to exchange views on risks and benefits related to AI. The next exchange will occur by November 2026.
– CNN’s Stephanie Yang, Issy Ronald and Sylvie Zhang contributed reporting.

The high-altitude reconnaissance platform took part in exercises around the disputed South China Sea flashpoint
Beijing deployed its advanced WZ-7 high-altitude reconnaissance drone in the South China Sea for the first time during drills near the disputed Scarborough Shoal on Sunday.
The People’s Liberation Army’s Southern Theatre Command announced on Sunday that it had conducted joint air and naval exercises in the waters and airspace around the shoal earlier in the day.
In recent years, Scarborough Shoal – known as Huangyan Island in China and Panatag Shoal in the Philippines – has been a major flashpoint between the two countries, which both claim ownership of the coral atoll.

Penalties and turnovers plagued New England in a 35-6 loss on Sunday.
After a Marcus Jones interception early in the second quarter awarded the New England Patriots a new set of downs at the Jacksonville Jaguars’ 21-yard line, trailing 7-0, the Patriots offense unraveled before they could run a full play.
On first down, right tackle Morgan Moses was called for a holding penalty that wiped out a Drake Maye scrambling touchdown. Then, a Romeo Doubs offensive pass interference call quickly followed that mishap, pushing New England back to a 1st-and-30 possession and forcing the offense to settle for a field goal.
That sequence was an early glimpse of the sloppy, undisciplined football on Sunday afternoon that plagued the Patriots in their dismal 35-6 road loss to the Jaguars.
“My concern level is very high for this football team,” head coach Mike Vrabel said after the contest. “When you come off a game like that, you just want to get back to work … We have to fix a lot of things.”
New England committed nine penalties throughout the matchup. While Jacksonville wasn’t far behind with seven of its own, the Patriots repeatedly made mistakes that prevented them from capitalizing on the Jaguars’ shortcomings.
Trailing just before halftime, but with a larger disparity at 14-3, Maye and his unit had an opportunity to at least cut the game to one score with a third-and-goal snap two yards out from the end zone. However, instead of settling for another three points, the quarterback forced a throw to a smothered Efton Chism III in the back of the painted area, allowing Jacksonville cornerback Travis Hunter to intercept the pass.
Maye was responsible for all three of New England’s turnovers stemming from poor decision-making when dropping back to pass and a jarring fumble that slipped from his hand on a pass attempt.
Still, Vrabel believes that resolving those mistakes begins with himself.
“We haven’t made good decisions with the football,” Vrabel added. “We have to get it fixed. We have to practice. We have to work and get it corrected. And everybody else has to do much better, and it starts with me. That’s how it goes … I need to get guys in there to do the things the way that we need them done.
“There are going to be mistakes, but there are too many things that get us beat: turnovers and not taking advantage of [Jacksonville’s] turnover opportunities.”
Following Maye’s final interception in the third frame, the team’s body language noticeably shifted, with the defense losing its physicality as the game progressed and the offense continuously failing to score.
That body language was evident at all three levels. After the Jaguars extended their lead to 28-3, Kyle Williams, instead of letting the ball roll out of bounds on the ensuing kickoff to accept a penalty, caught the kick, pinning the Patriots at their own nine.
“I think it’s one day at a time,” Vrabel said. “It’s about what we can do to get healthy and improve individually and as a football team. That’s all we can do. It’s going to start with me and my ability to teach and get the guys in the right spots.”
New England, dropping to 1-2 on the season, will travel to Buffalo next week to face the undefeated Bills in a crucial divisional game.

articles.title_orig: US and China list goods for tariff cuts – what it means for Europe
articles.title_zh: US and China list goods for tariff cuts – what it means for Europe
articles.content_orig:
The United States and China have unveiled a list of goods recommended for reduced tariffs following last week’s summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping.
The release of the list on Sunday comes after Trump and Xi agreed to work towards lowering tariffs on $60bn worth of trade.
The agreement, which covers $30bn of each side’s imports, identifies 77 Chinese goods and more than 1,600 US products to be considered for more favourable tariff treatment.
Chinese goods on the list include microwave ovens, fish hooks, artificial flowers and weighing scales.
US exports identified for lower tariffs include poultry, dairy products, noodles, eggs, peanuts, canned tomatoes, pure-breed breeding horses, and silk.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the agreement would improve market access for about 30 percent of US exports to China and also benefit US consumers.
“The Trump Administration will continue to pursue fair, balanced, and reciprocal trade with China by ensuring compliance with commitments on agricultural and energy purchases, pursuing balanced trade in non-sensitive goods, and securing market access for American farmers, manufacturers, businesses, and workers,” Greer said in a statement.
China’s Ministry of Commerce, which confirmed the list on Monday, shortly after the White House announcement, said the sides would discuss “a reciprocal tariff reduction framework of $30 billion for $30 billion, aiming to reach a consensus”.
“This arrangement will help stabilize China-US trade, create better conditions for Chinese exports of relevant products to the US, meet domestic market demand, and strengthen trade cooperation in agricultural products, energy, manufactured goods, and consumer goods,” the ministry said in a statement.
While Trump and Xi’s summit was heavy on pomp and ceremony, their talks wrapped up on Friday with few concrete announcements on the myriad divisions between the superpower rivals, which span everything from trade to artificial intelligence and Taiwan.
Trump and Xi, who have held three face-to-face summits since last October, are expected to meet again at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, and the Group of 20 gathering in Miami, Florida, in December.
Trade between the US and China, the world’s two largest economies, has declined substantially since Trump, a longtime critic of free trade policies, returned to the White House in January last year.
Two-way trade totalled $495bn in 2025, down 25 percent from the previous year, according to the US Trade Representative.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore, said the latest announcement did not point to a major shift in US-China trade.
“Instead, both sides have largely listed goods that do not move the needle on overall trade flows,” Elms told Al Jazeera.
“They may reduce some prices in the US for consumers, but none is going to make a dramatic difference in inflation figures or result in meaningful sighs of relief by most US buyers,” Elms added.
“The same is broadly true with the Chinese list. Although there are many different agricultural products on the list, most are not actually exported to China or not exported in meaningful quantities.”

Nvidia ( NVDA ) released the Open Agent Safety Platform, which is aimed at helping AI developers enforce safeguards for agents, a few days after the AI hardware giant's CEO questioned the security approaches of Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) and OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ).
"AI's extraordinary potential for society will only be realized if we solve AI safety," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang stated in a press release. "As we continue to discover the frontier of AI capabilities, we must accelerate discovery at the frontier of AI safety. Safety and security require full-stack engineering."
Last week, Huang sat down with Ezra Klein of The New York Times to discuss recent warnings from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman suggesting that the pace of AI development could threaten humanity.
"If your product is not ready to ship, don't ship the product," Huang told The Ezra Klein Show podcast. "This is the first time that I've heard a company or CEO say that I need … the liability laws of products to be relieved so that I can pace myself."
Huang repeatedly described the stance of the leading AI labs as "odd," given that those companies are leading AI innovation while the safety risks, in his view, can be mitigated with technology.
"Nobody is building more compute today than the people asking to be slowed down," Huang told Klein. "It strikes me as odd. … I know a lot of people in those two labs who are dedicating their lives to do good work. They know what happened. I know they know what happened. I know they know how to fix it, and I know they're fixing it."
Read more: AI isn't coming to destroy humanity, but experts say the real threats are here
The new safety platform is aimed at establishing security protocols that could prevent alarming breaches from being unveiled by the frontier labs.
"NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform brings together industry, researchers and public-sector organizations to share best practices, align on evaluation methods and foster international cooperation," Huang added in the press release. "Together, we can raise the bar for global AI safety."
Speaking with Klein, Huang suggested that the AI labs simply rebalance their priorities.
"So when I say we need to accelerate AI technology, people think, for some reason, that safety is not part of that," the Nvidia CEO said . "Safety is part of it. Alignment is part of it. Evaluation is part of it: Guardrailing, sandboxing, the isolation technology, monitoring technology, telemetry technology, external A.I. monitor technology — all of that stuff is A.I. technology. Accelerate the living daylights out of that."
Klein noted that "if the most alarmed people at the labs could be assured they were going to move 80 percent of their compute into safety and alignment, as opposed to 80 percent into capability expansion, they would feel much better."
Huang replied: "Yeah, what's stopping them from doing it?"

articles.title_orig: The Xbox Series X Can Now Play PlayStation 5 Games - Here's How
articles.title_zh: The Xbox Series X Can Now Play PlayStation 5 Games - Here's How
articles.content_orig:
Certain PlayStation 5 games are now running on Xbox Series X hardware thanks to a new emulator developed by the modding community. While the latest PS5 games, like "Marvel's Wolverine," won't be running on Xbox anytime soon, there's been a surprising amount of progress made with PS5 emulation on PC — and that progress is slowly being transferred to emulation on Xbox.
The root of this project is KytyPS5, an open-source PlayStation 5 emulator for PC. A modder named Devran Cosmo Uenal built a special port of the emulator for Xbox Series X, calling this new version PS5X. It's not quite up to par with KytyPS5 on PC, but the results are already impressive.
Multiple PS5 games are somewhat playable on PS5X, complete with Xbox inputs and a fancy user interface to swap between titles. The experience isn't perfect by any means, but they're semi-playable with minor glitches and performance problems — a remarkable achievement for experimental emulation in such an early state.
Currently, only a handful of small PS5 games are playable on PS5X. Uenal's YouTube page features a PS5X library with "Gex Trilogy," "Hellboy: Web of Wyrd," "Marvel Cosmic Invasion," and "Quake 2.' Smaller games like these are typically the first to reach playable states with new emulators, but things can improve fast. Just look at Nintendo Switch emulation on Android , for example.
PS5X is still in a very early state, and the gameplay footage recorded by Uenal shows "Quake 2" running at an inconsistent framerate, bouncing between 20 and 40 FPS. It's impressive that the PS5 version of "Quake 2" is running on Xbox hardware at all, but PS5X still needs a lot of work if it's going to run big PS5 exclusives like "Demon's Souls" or "Ghost of Yotei."
Work seems to be progressing quickly on PS5X, however. A new user interface update posted by Uenal shows "Crash Bandicoot 4: It's About Time," "Grand Theft Auto 5," and "Gran Turismo 7" as new additions to his library, indicating that these games are being tested. When PS5X releases publicly, you'll be able to install and test it yourself by putting your Xbox in developer mode. And don't worry — it's totally safe, and you won't brick your Xbox Series X by doing so.
PS5X is behind right now because KytyPS5 uses Vulkan rendering on PC, but the Xbox Series X doesn't support it. Everything has to be manually translated to DirectX to work on Xbox, which hurts compatibility and performance. If you're eager to test out PS5 emulation and you have a powerful gaming PC , you can check out KytyPS5 to get a sneak peek at some of the features and performance improvements that'll come to PS5X down the line.
KytyPS5 has made significant breakthroughs in recent months, and progress shows no signs of slowing down. "Astro Bot" and "Demon's Souls" can both run without crashing, and while the framerate dips down into the single digits, this is still an impressive achievement for PS5 emulation. Since PS5X is a port of KytyPS5, these advancements will likely come to PS5X later on if work continues on the project.
PlayStation 5 emulation continues to grow at a rapid pace on PC, meaning big games like "Grand Theft Auto 5" might be the next titles to run on PS5X. "GTA 5" is surprisingly playable on KytyPS5 with high-end PC hardware, and Uenal had the game installed on PS5X in his user interface showcase video. It'll just take time to optimize things specifically for the Xbox port of the emulator.

articles.content_orig:
The United States and China have released lists of products worth about $30 billion each that will see tariff cuts
HONG KONG -- The United States and China released Monday reciprocal lists of products worth about $30 billion each that will see tariff cuts, in a deal expected to boost bilateral trade.
The details came days after Chinese President Xi Jinping met with President Donald Trump in Washington in his first state visit to the U.S. since 2015. The U.S. had already reduced tariffs against China after Trump’s tariffs reached as high as 145% at one point last year, as tensions between the two countries eased.
China’s commerce ministry said in a statement the agreement will help strengthen trade cooperation.
The lists included 1,619 items of U.S. goods entering China, ranging from agricultural commodities, personal care products to timber and medical equipment. Coal from the U.S. will also be included.
For Chinese goods exported to the U.S., 77 categories were covered, including fireworks, tableware, glass and wooden Christmas ornaments and soccer balls.
Tariff rates on over 90% of the products would be subject to “most-favored-nation” levels, the Chinese commerce ministry said, meaning that country-specific tariffs will effectively be eliminated.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a separate statement the product lists focused on “nonsensitive goods on each side that could benefit from more favorable tariff treatment.” The deal could help secure market access for U.S. farmers, manufacturers, businesses and workers, while benefiting American consumers with imports from China including household goods and toys, Greer said.
Both countries said they agreed the list may be adjusted later as needed, but amendments were likely to be no more than on an annual basis.
The Chinese commerce ministry said the two countries agreed to further cooperate in the agricultural sector, forming a group under the Board of Trade established in May to optimize bilateral trade.
Sectors of strategic importance for both countries, such as chips , electric vehicles and batteries, were not covered under the agreement.
“This is a positive outcome for these affected products compared to a smaller tariff cut, and could lead to a more significant boost to bilateral trade,” said Lynn Song, chief economist for Greater China at ING Bank.
The lowered tariffs could be a win for U.S. consumer brands, added Jacob Cooke, CEO of WPIC Marketing + Technologies based in Beijing, as some of the products covered by China's list of U.S. imports included fast-growing categories like hair care, personal care products and infant formula.
The U.S. list for Chinese imports focused more on consumer goods, which could help lower U.S. inflation while also allowing Chinese firms to export more of their overcapacity, said Gary Ng, a senior economist at French bank Natixis.
Some experts said, however, the economic impact at $30 billion each way may be limited overall.
U.S. exports to China were roughly $68 billion through the first seven months of this year, while Chinese exports to the U.S. were at around $270 billion for the first eight months, said Prashant Bhayani, chief investment officer for Asia at BNP Paribas Wealth Management.
A $30 billion deal each way will be “more meaningful” for U.S. exports to China in terms of percentage share, he said.
While the deal did not cover sensitive strategic goods, analysts believe U.S.-China trade will likely continue to recover for the rest of the year after steep U.S. tariffs on Chinese products last year hit bilateral trade.
The U.S. and China last week also reached a two-month extension of the broader trade truce that was set to expire Nov. 10 to January.
China’s trade surplus, which reached a record $1.2 trillion last year, will likely remain elevated. By August, it stood at about $800 billion, putting this year’s surplus “on pace to exceed the 2025 record,” according to Ecaterina Bigos, a senior market strategist with BNP Paribas Asset Management.
The U.S. is also investigating China among 16 trading partners in its Section 301 probe on excess industrial capacity and could impose additional tariffs on China when the investigation concludes.
However, with more meetings set between Trump and Xi, including at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen in November and at the Group of 20 summit in Florida in December, Song at ING said he would not expect a major flare-up of trade tensions before year-end.
Some Chinese exporters welcomed the tariff deal announcements.
“This is positive news,” said Richard Chan of Golden Arts Gifts & Decor, which manufactures Christmas decorations in southern China and supplies to countries including the U.S. “The economy in both the U.S. and China is not really good, and the two sides should help each other more.”
However, because most of this year’s Christmas goods are already being shipped ahead of the peak holiday season, the tariff reductions may have limited effect for them at least for now.

articles.title_orig: Bangkok’s flood disaster – in pictures | Thailand
articles.title_zh: Bangkok’s flood disaster – in pictures | Thailand
articles.content_orig:
Capital city submerged in waist-high flood water, while elsewhere Hurricane Nolo threatens Hawaii’s Big Island
Bangkok was declared a disaster zone by its city officials towards the end of last week, after streets in Thailand’s capital city were submerged in up to waist-high flood water. The flooding stemmed from an active cell of low pressure across central Thailand that brought continuous heavy rainfall and thunderstorms to Bangkok and surrounding regions.
The heavy rain began early on Thursday when the weak area of low pressure travelled north-westwards up the gulf of Thailand before then sitting over central Thailand by Friday morning. For most of the following two days this low pressure remained roughly in situ, which allowed unrelenting downpours over Bangkok and nearby areas. One weather station near Prachin Buri, just north-east of the capital, recorded 213.5mm within a 24-hour period between Friday and Saturday evening local time – for comparison, London receives an average 585mm a year ). Fortunately, the centre of the low-pressure cell shifted north-westwards on Sunday and brought an end to the torrential rainfall.
Out in the central Pacific, meanwhile, citizens of Hawaii’s Big Island were threatened by Hurricane Nolo over the weekend. The system initially approached the archipelago early last week, bringing heavy rainfall from around Tuesday evening. By the early hours of Saturday Nolo was a category 2 hurricane, with sustained windspeeds of 85-90knots (98-104mph), situated at its closest to the archipelago at approximately 145 miles (233km) south of the Big Island. Strong winds were not the only threat to the Big Island, as the vast quantity of rainfall raised concerns over flooding and mudslides. Since the impacts of Nolo started late on Tuesday 22 September, weather stations in the north-east of the island have received over 530mm of rainfall. Fortunately, Nolo has propagated westwards away from Hawaii where it is forecast to peak in its intensity on Monday 28 September, with current predictions of achieving category 4 status.
after newsletter promotion
Meanwhile, farther east in the Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Polo is now forecast to make landfall with the Baja California peninsula late in the day on Monday 28 September. The once category 5 hurricane will downgrade to category 2 by landfall with sustained winds of 96-110mph. A hurricane warning has been issued in coastal regions due to the risk of a storm surge where winds are onshore. Polo will also bring intense downpours while traversing the peninsula with 100-200mm expected, potentially reaching up to 250mm locally. The bulk of this rain falling within a 12-hour period and bringing the risk of life-threatening flooding and mudslides. The storm will continue to weaken while propagating north-eastwards across the Sonora region in Mexico.

articles.title_orig: After a Life in Isolation, a Tennessee Woman Waits for Her Execution
articles.title_zh: After a Life in Isolation, a Tennessee Woman Waits for Her Execution
articles.content_orig:
Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.
Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed.
"She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.
Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.
Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.
Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.
Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.
Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".
Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder [Family handout]
But Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped.
Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.
In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider.
"It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence.
"Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."
Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parents [Christa Pike]
In 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.
But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.
In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.
Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her.
"Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.
Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."
Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."
Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say [Christa Pike]
Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.
A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict.
The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.
Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021 .
Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before.
The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.
On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.
Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution.
"She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.
Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."
May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006 [J. Miles Carey/USA TODAY/Imagn Images via Reuters]
"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added.
"There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."
The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.
The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want.
"We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."
Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption.
"When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says.

articles.title_zh: The Apple Next Vision Pro Is Reportedly on ‘Life Support’
articles.content_orig:
Apple is working on a "completely revamped" Vision Pro headset that could go in any of four directions and likely won't arrive before late 2028 or early 2029, according to Bloomberg 's Mark Gurman.
Writing in his latest Power On newsletter , Gurman said Apple's Vision team is exploring four concepts for the device, codenamed N224, including designs that offload internal components in a similar way to Meta's latest VR Glasses , which are expected to launch next spring.
An external computing module on Meta's device houses the battery and main processor, and can be clipped to the user's waist. Gurman, who has previewed Meta's headset, says the module is about the same size and weight as the current Vision Pro's battery pack, but with a grippy exterior.
Gurman reports that regardless of the Vision team's work, senior Apple decision-makers still consider the external puck concept as a "poor user experience" and want the company to stick with "something closer to an all-in-one design."
If any of this sounds familiar, that's because Gurman reported in June that Apple was still working on a cheaper, lighter successor to its Vision Pro headset. (The device-in-development is distinct from the long-rumored "Vision Air," which was cancelled last year .)
Apple knows it needs to come up with ways to simplify the design and make something cheaper and lighter, and it is said to be actively exploring ways to reduce the headset's weight by experimenting with plastic, titanium, other metals and various materials.
Still, Gurman has been told the work is on "life support" as the company focuses more on smart glasses, which it aims to release in late 2027. Despite the Vision Pro's most senior leaders "pressing their bosses to keep the category alive, funded and growing at Apple," Gurman says there's still no guarantee a new headset will ever launch.

ByteDance accounts for roughly one-fifth of China’s delivered data centre capacity, making the TikTok owner the country’s largest tenant and a main driver of its artificial intelligence buildout, according to new estimates by research firm SemiAnalysis.

Its AI products include Doubao, an assistant that ByteDance says has hundreds of millions of users, and Seedance, a video generation model.
While ByteDance’s financials remain undisclosed as a private company, capital spending by its listed peers has surged. Alibaba Group Holding, Tencent Holdings and Baidu spent a combined US$20 billion on capital expenditure in the second quarter, more than double the figure from a year earlier, according to the report published on Friday. All three tech giants posted negative free cash flow in the same quarter for the first time on record.

articles.title_orig: Parents confront a new fear: Could AI end humanity before their kids grow up?
articles.title_zh: Parents confront a new fear: Could AI end humanity before their kids grow up?
articles.content_orig:
Molly Kinder saw the apocalyptic warnings about artificial intelligence while walking home from dropping her children off at elementary school. Scrolling through social media posts where AI insiders were issuing dire claims that the technology could cause human extinction , she stopped dead in her tracks just a block from the doorway where she had just hugged her 4-year-old goodbye.
A former Brookings Institute researcher who left to start an organization focused on AI’s impacts on jobs, Kinder was well-versed in its potential to disrupt society. But in that moment, on a September morning in Washington, DC, she didn’t react to the news as a policy wonk or someone with ties to the AI world. Instead, said Kinder, “I immediately reacted to it as a mother.”
“As soon as I became a mom, my number one task was to nurture these kids and keep them alive – just like every other parent out there, just like any animal,” said the 46-year-old mother of three, who cleared her schedule that morning to write about her fears in a lengthy thread on X. “It’s a biological instinct. This is the first time I genuinely felt truly afraid of some external thing outside my control.”
Long a topic of discussion in Silicon Valley and AI circles, concerns that superintelligent machines could eventually pose an existential risk to humanity have gone mainstream in recent months. First, OpenAI revealed that a swarm of its experimental AI models broke out of a testing environment and hacked another AI platform, Hugging Face, without human direction or knowledge. Then came a social media post from a young Anthropic researcher named Jacob Coxon , announcing he was leaving the industry due to his belief that the companies behind AI “are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Others in the industry echoed the concern – with one Anthropic researcher citing his own view that there was a more than 10 percent chance that future models could “kill all humans!” within the next decade.
Suddenly, a theoretical risk that’s been espoused by some of the so-called “godfathers of AI,” been warned about in statements endorsed by leading researchers and been studied by AI companies exploded into the broader public’s consciousness.
Will AI really kill everyone? How, exactly?
Leading AI executives, many of whom agree the technology poses dangers to human survival, called for a slowdown in the pace of development. And politicians began debating whether legislation is needed to rein in an industry that is racing against China and expected to drive enormous profits and technological advancements.
By early this month, polls were finding that 64 percent of Americans believed it was somewhat or very likely that AI could become powerful enough to pose a serious threat to humanity’s survival. That potential, however remote, landed hard for a group especially invested in the future of humanity: moms.
Liz Black, a 41-year-old writer who lives outside Philadelphia, had thought hard about whether to have a child, contemplating concerns like climate change. What helped solidify her decision to go for it was a line her mother wrote while making her own choice about having kids: “Life is worth repeating.” Black found the message after her death and was so moved she got it tattooed on her arm.
When she had her son three and a half years ago, superintelligent computers ending humanity was not on her radar. Recently, she said, it’s been “a low-level hum in the back of my mind constantly.” The situation feels out of control to her – like “a small number of companies, a small number of people, are holding us all hostage.” She is determined to not allow herself to be consumed by the what-ifs, instead focusing on the son who sings to her and repeats her reminders to be gentle to other kids.
“I need to believe that there is a future for myself and my husband and my child,” Black said.
While some are dismissive of the existential panic, believing it to be overblown or a distraction from current-day AI issues, others have found themselves grappling with new questions about what it means to bring life into the world – and what kind of action is required in the face of a potentially catastrophic future. They’ve flocked to online forums in search of advice and support, posting things like, “I am constantly questioning reality, wondering what’s the point, feeling guilty for bringing my child into this world.” They’ve shared podcasts and news articles in group chats, gauging whether they are getting sucked into exaggerated hypotheticals or if they’re right to worry.
One woman, poet and comedian Hayley DeRoche, took to Instagram with a poem that seemed to capture the surrealness of the moment: “What do we even do/Like/We knew our kids didn’t have futures already but this?” She titled it, “My Mom Group Worries About AI Causing a Mass Human Extinction Event.”
AI researcher and professor David Krueger, who has been sounding the alarm for years, said he has tried to imagine how it must feel for those who are now realizing the gamble being made by frontier AI companies. He doesn’t have kids, in part because of his concern about what will happen if humans lose control of AI systems, but said, “I think parents’ feeling of wanting to protect their kids is one of the strongest forces in the world.”
“I think I’d just be so outraged and upset at people who are just very apparently, very brazenly and callously risking my kid’s life,” added Krueger, an assistant professor of computer science at the University of Montreal.
It’s long been his position that the existential threat is real – that if companies continue racing to make AI more autonomous and more intelligent, human control could be lost, with the disappearance of humankind likely to follow. As an assistant professor at the University of Cambridge in 2023, he initiated a one-sentence statement on the extinction risk signed by prominent AI researchers and industry leaders. Last year, he founded a nonprofit called Evitable to inform and activate the public on the dangers of developing more powerful AI systems.
Watching the world outside the AI bubble start talking about the existential threat, Krueger said he’s felt the most optimistic than he can remember being in the more than 15 years he has worried about the risk to humanity. To him, the next step is clear: stop developing more autonomous, more powerful AI systems as soon as possible.
“People often talk about this as a race between the US and China,” Krueger said. “I think about it as a race between people rushing to build this dangerous technology and people becoming activated and racing to stop them.”
Not everyone thinks AI will kill us all
Some in the AI world have downplayed the danger, casting doomsday predictions as more science fiction than scientific or arguing that the risks can be managed. Even among researchers and insiders who believe there is a risk the technology could one day wipe out humanity, there is no widespread agreement on when – or how – that would happen. The general idea, as Yoshua Bengio, one of the “godfathers of AI,” has put it , is that if machines become smarter than humans, they will develop their own agency and goals that are potentially different than their creators intended. Many AI developers believe the danger can be mitigated through “alignment,” or working to imbue AI systems with human values, but Krueger, Bengio and others do not think current alignment techniques can guarantee safety.
Concern over the way the technology can impact children isn’t new, although the focus has generally been on how its use can hinder learning or harm mental health. Julie Scelfo, a New York-based journalist and mother of three who founded MAMA – Mothers Against Media Addiction, said her organization’s attitude is “let’s focus on the actual harms that are happening – let’s get those under control, and in doing so, we will be protecting future generations.” She’s more worried a

Ministry of State Security warns citizens not to be lured by ‘illusion’ of anonymous transactions
China’s top intelligence and security agency on Monday issued a stark new warning on the risks of cryptocurrencies, highlighting their role in crime and stressing that transactions are not anonymous.
Here are three things to know about the fresh warning from the Ministry of State Security (MSS) and China’s latest stance on virtual assets.
Virtual currencies facilitated money laundering activities and cyberattacks, and served as “accomplices” in espionage, the agency said in an article published on its social media account. Overseas intelligence agencies would try to dispel the concerns of people they were trying to recruit as spies by claiming that the circulation of virtual currencies was hard to verify, according to the Ministry.
The MSS described the anonymity of crypto transactions as a “false proposition” and an “illusion”, saying that blockchains could fully retain transaction records and that exchanges between crypto and fiat currencies, as well as other payment interfaces, made real identities hard to hide.
Crypto was often used by “overseas anti-China hostile forces” for activities that disrupted financial order and harmed national security, it said, adding that crypto businesses were illegal in China.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving
articles.title_zh: Nvidia releases software platform to stop AI agents from misbehaving
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia is rolling out a new software platform to allow AI developers to set safeguards for agents and prevent them from breaking out of containment.
The release on Monday of Nvidia's Open Agent Safety Platform comes after companies including OpenAI , Anthropic , Meta , and Google disclosed recent incidents in which their artificial intelligence models escaped their sandboxes and attempted to hack other companies and access their computer systems.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Monday that it is essentially the modern browser, "a browser for agents."
"You can't have agents roam around and drift around the company, and so you have to find a way to container it," Huang told CNBC.
An Nvidia representative told reporters on a call on Sunday that its platform could have prevented OpenAI's Hugging Face incident in July. That's when OpenAI models escaped containment, accessed the open internet and breached Hugging Face, which operates an open-source developer platform.
"Each security incident is unique, and we have to look at all of them in detail," said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, the world's most valuable company. "From what we know, Hugging Face reported over 17,000 agents attacking their infrastructure that went on for days and weeks."
Nvidia has been at the center of the generative AI boom since the launch of ChatGPT almost four years ago, as the chipmaker's graphics processing units are critical to the development of large language models and to the AI services offered by hyperscalers. But Huang has more recently emerged as a key voice in the AI safety debate, arguing that many security concerns are engineering issues that can be solved through computer science and product development.
"You have to think about what you could have done, what's the solution for it,"  Huang said in a podcast with The New York Times' Ezra Klein released last week, referring to recent incidents. "In the future, improve your process so that you could avoid this from happening again."
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei set off an industry firestorm two weeks ago, urging AI model developers to slow their pace of advancement due to fears of the models spinning out of control, an argument that was supported by OpenAI's Sam Altman and SpaceX's Elon Musk .
Nvidia's new offering is an engineering solution to the agent safety issue, Boitano said.
"Recent incidents have highlighted a fundamental hurdle for AI agents, and that is that model-level safeguards alone can't govern what agents can access or do," Boitano said.
One component of the platform is called Nvidia OpenShell, which runs on central processors and sets limits on agent capabilities. Nvidia also announced Sentry, which monitors agents and runs on network chips, not CPUs or GPUs.
Some of the software is open source, and Nvidia is calling its platform a reference design, which means partners are intended to build products on top of it to bring it to market.
Nvidia named Cisco , Microsoft , Oracle , CoreWeave , Dell , HPE , Lenovo, ARM and Intel as partners. Nvidia is also working with Anthropic to integrate cloud managed agents with OpenShell.
"We can't have a successful AI industry if the world doesn't think it's built or confident that it's built and deployed safely," Huang told CNBC on Monday.

articles.title_orig: What to know about the $810 million in spending canceled by President Trump
articles.title_zh: What to know about the $810 million in spending canceled by President Trump
articles.content_orig:
Democrats are blaming Office of Management and Budget director Russell Vought for the canceled funds, accusing him of violating the separation of powers and undermining Congressional authority. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images North America hide caption
Each year, Congress passes laws which allocate money to the federal government's various programs and agencies. Trump, for the second year in a row, is refusing to send some of that money to the places that Congress says it has to go , setting off a fresh battle with lawmakers over who controls federal spending.
Of the $810 million being withheld, $567 million comes from programs that "provided services to refugees, asylees, and other non-citizens," according to a memo from the White House.
The move, called a pocket rescission, is illegal, according to the Government Accountability Office , an independent, non-partisan watchdog agency charged with providing federal agencies fact-based information.
Article 1 of the Constitution gives Congress t he power to levy taxes and decide how federal funds are spent — known as power of the purse. If the president disagrees, he or she can send a request to Congress to cancel the fund, but that is supposed to happen with 45 days notice in order to let Congress agree or disagree.
A pocket rescission happens when the president decides to cancel funds without ample time for Congress to weigh in or reallocate the money. With the end of the fiscal year less than a week away, the announcement means the funds will go unspent and Congress can't respond.
"This is the most recent attempt by this Office of Management and Budget (OMB) to undermine Congress's Constitutional power of the purse," Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, who chairs the Senate Appropriations committee, wrote in a statement posted to X. "OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding."
The canceled funds are fueling anger from Democrats who say OMB director Russell Vought is violating the separation of powers and undermining Congressional authority.
"This is theft from the American people, plain and simple," wrote Washington Sen. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee on X. "Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because Vought is saying their votes don't count."
"Donald Trump knows he can't get these cuts through Congress, so he is illegally making them through the back door," Rep. Brendan Boyle, the top Democrat on the House Budget committee, said in a statement. "Trump's actions are a blatant attack on Congress's constitutional power of the purse."
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
The administration also says it withheld $15 million to a Justice Department team tasked with "preventing and resolving racial and ethnic tensions, incidents, and civil disorders, and in restoring racial stability and harmony," $70 million to "programs provide grants and fellowships to support institutions bringing foreign students and faculty to the United States to study or teach language," and tens of millions to various research and non-profit grant programs that target climate change or racial and gender minority work.
A detailed accounting provided by the administration can be found here .

articles.title_zh: ‘Avengers: Endgame’ retakes box office crown; Robert Pattinson drives sales for ‘Primetime’
articles.content_orig:
NEW YORK — Seven years after becoming the second-highest grossing film ever, “Avengers: Endgame” returned to the No. 1 spot at the box office in a victory lap for Marvel and an appetizer for the upcoming blockbuster “Avengers: Doomsday.”
The rerelease grossed $26 million over the weekend and another $60 million overseas, according to studio estimates Sunday. The film, which grossed $2.8 billion in 2019, was put back into theaters with several new end-credits scenes and an introductory thank you to fans from Robert Downey Jr. and Chris Evans.
Among rereleases, only the 1997 release of “Star Wars: A New Hope” ($35.9 million) and the 2011 repeat of “The Lion King” ($30.2 million) have opened higher than “Endgame” in domestic cinemas.
Hollywood has increasingly turned to rereleases in recent years to take advantage of holes in the release schedule. But The Walt Disney Co. rerun, billed as “Endgame: Encore,” came out on top on an especially crowded weekend in theaters.
Three well-reviewed new releases — A24’s “Primetime,” with Robert Pattinson; Paramount Pictures’ “Heart of the Beast,” with Brad Pitt; and Universal Pictures’ “Forgotten Island” — all landed in theaters.
Second place, though, went to Zach Cregger’s reboot of “Resident Evil.” The Sony Pictures release followed up its above-expectations debut with $23.3 million in its second weekend. In two weeks, the video-game adaptation has grossed $103.5 million in U.S. and Canadian theaters.
In a close race for third place, “Heart of the Beast” came out just ahead of “Primetime” with an estimated $20 million from 3,435 theaters. Directed by David Ayer, the film stars Pitt as a retired veteran who must trek through the Alaskan wilderness with his combat dog after a plane crash. It added $30.1 million in international theaters.
But the opening for “Primetime” was more impressive. “Heart of the Beast” cost $82 million to produce, making its path to profitability challenging. “Primetime,” starring Pattinson as “To Catch a Predator” host Chris Hansen, was made with a modest budget of $15 million and it opened in 500 fewer theaters.
Yet “Primetime,” buoyed by strong reviews and buzz out of the Venice Film Festival , debuted with $19.2 million. For Pattinson, who also starred this year in A24’s “The Drama” and Universal’s “The Odyssey,” the strong performance showed the actor’s drawing power with Gen Z audiences.
Some 69% of ticket buyers for “Primetime” were under the age of 30. Gen Z has emerged as the most regular moviegoing demographic, fueling hits this year like “Obsession” and “Backrooms.” “Primetime” is directed by 30-year-old documentarian Lance Oppenheim, who co-directed the much-anticipated Elizabeth Holmes documentary, “You Can See Everything,” due out next month.
“Forgotten Island,” from DreamWorks Animation, had a hard time standing out. The film, which cost $80 million to make, opened in fifth place with a disappointing $12.8 million domestically. In 31 overseas markets, “Forgotten Island” also didn’t make much of a dent, grossing $7.8 million internationally.
Universal will hope family audiences catch up to the movie that landed the weekend’s best CinemaScore (an “A”) and the best reviews (94% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes). “Forgotten Island,” directed by Joel Crawford and Januel Mercado, is about two friends who get stranded in a mystical world.
The confluence of releases added up to a historically good September weekend in theaters. According to Rentrak, ticket sales were up 58.5% from the same weekend last year. The domestic box office has massed $7.8 billion thus far, putting it 19% ahead of last year.
With final domestic figures being released Monday, this list factors in the estimated ticket sales for Friday through Sunday at U.S. and Canadian theaters, according to Rentrak:
1. “Avengers: Endgame: Encore,” $26 million.
2. “Resident Evil,” $23.3 million.
3. “Heart of the Beast,” $20 million.
4. “Primetime,” $19.2 million.
5. “Forgotten Island,” $12.8 million.
6. “Practical Magic 2,” $5.7 million.

8. “The Odyssey,” $3.7 million.
9. “Coyote vs. Acme,” $1.9 million.
