articles.title_zh: Tom Kean Jr. Backs Trump on Iran and Tariffs, if Not Local Issues
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
NEW YORK — President Trump threatened to “annihilate” Iran  if it fails to negotiate a deal over its nuclear program, delivering a defensive speech justifying the mission at the United Nations on Tuesday.
His remarks come more than six months into a war that has grown increasingly unpopular at home, with fewer than a third of Americans approving of the president’s handling of the conflict, according to recent polls.
“I have a big decision to make,” he told world leaders gathered at the U.N. General Assembly in New York, with Iranian diplomats in attendance.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before — maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic, and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy again?
“Do I drive them into hell,” he continued, “with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness?”
The war has carried steep political costs for the president and his party ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November, increasing inflation and energy prices due to disruptions in commercial shipping traffic through key waterways in the Middle East.
Defense officials say the conflict has also placed a huge burden on U.S. munitions stockpiles, as Iran continues firing ballistic missiles and drones at American assets and bases throughout the region.
But Trump denied that the war has depleted U.S. stocks. “That’s not true,” he said.
“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election,” Trump said. “We must be equally united in maintaining pressure.”
The rise in global gas prices has sparked protests around the world. But Trump’s vow to ensure Tehran never acquires a nuclear weapon — an issue that for decades united the international community — generated applause throughout the chamber.
The president’s actions stand to color the backdrop of a week that will feature meetings with world leaders at the U.N. and a state visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Launching  the war on Iran in February, Trump projected the campaign would last roughly six weeks, with the stated objective of disabling Iran’s ballistic missile program, its navy and its nuclear infrastructure. He also vowed a day would soon come when the Iranian people could rise up against their government and reclaim their country.
More than six months later, the Islamic Republic stands. Iran’s ballistic missiles continue to test U.S. air defenses across the Middle East, shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains depressed, and talks over the future of Iran’s nuclear program have collapsed.
Explaining his decision to start the war, Trump said that he decided not to let the problem of Iran’s nuclear work “fester,” and warned that its ballistic missile program was being designed as a shield to protect its nuclear program from foreign attack.
“Iran’s goal was to complete their mad dash to a nuclear bomb from behind this conventional ballistic missile shield,” Trump said. “They were the bully of the Middle East, but they’re the bully no more.”
He said the United States has repeatedly offered Iran a deal  that would open up economic cooperation between the two nations in exchange for an end to  Iran’s nuclear work. “They absolutely refused,” he added. “That was a big mistake.”
U.S. and Iranian officials met on the sidelines of the annual general assembly, in a meeting Trump later described as productive.
“Very good meeting,” he told reporters traveling with him in New York. “I can’t imagine why they wouldn’t want to. It’s greatness, potential greatness, or obliteration.”
When outlining his priorities on the Western Hemisphere, Trump vowed to use “unmatched military might” when necessary if drug cartel activity in other countries poses a threat to the United States.
“Our actions in Venezuela are proof that the United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere,” Trump said.
Trump said his administration is reasserting its power over regional drug cartels, which he characterized as “the ISIS of the Western Hemisphere.” He said drug cartel members should be “killed, exiled  or detained as enemy combatants without the possibility of release,” and said Mexico was the “epicenter of the cartel violence.”
“Mexico must reclaim control of its soil from the enemies of humanity,” he said.
In the same remarks, Trump said his administration is seeking a “fundamental change” in Cuba, which he called a “failed state.” He said talks on what comes next for the communist island are being negotiated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
“It will fall,” he said, as members of the Cuban delegation walked out of the room.
Also in the room was Delcy Rodríguez, the acting president of Venezuela. She has worked closely with the Trump administration since the U.S. military captured Nicolás Maduro and brought him to the United States to face drug trafficking charges.
Rodríguez and Trump were expected to have a “pull aside” meeting, said Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations. Their encounter is the first time the two leaders met in person since Maduro’s capture.
Because Rodríguez is a holdover from the Maduro government, the meeting has drawn criticism in Venezuela, where many believe Trump is legitimizing her. Earlier this month, those tensions grew when the U.S. government entered an agreement with an oil producer to develop Venezuelan’s vast oil resources, with Rodríguez’s blessing.
The sweeping oil deal raised uncertainty about how entrenched the unelected government may become, more so after Trump said he did not think Venezuela was ready to hold democratic elections yet.
“It’s very new. We took them out of a dictatorship and we’re getting along great with the government,” Trump told reporters earlier this month. But he said an election would happen “soon.”
Also Tuesday, after months of threatening to seize Greenland , Trump signed a security agreement with the leaders of the Arctic territory and Denmark, one that he lauded as “tremendous for Europe and the United States.”
Details of the deal remained vague upon its signing. But Trump told the General Assembly that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all of the needs” of the Danish territory.
“We will have the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent and also Europe and other places,” Trump said.
The agreement would bar any U.S. adversaries from establishing a military presence in Greenland.
Mette Frederiksen, the Danish prime minister, on Tuesday said the accord “respects the sovereignty and the territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark as well as Greenland’s right to self-determination.”
Action is still needed by the Danish and Greenland governments before it can be enforced, though Trump characterized it as more immediate. He told the General Assembly that the United States planned to immediately grow its military presence in the Arctic island. The agreement says Denmark and Greenland will review U.S. requests to expand the military presence under “accelerated governmental approval procedures.”
“We will immediately begin the process of developing a large military presence in the appropriate locations,” he said. “We will be building two major military bases.”
Frederiksen told Trump on Tuesday that the deal would help protect the United States from foreign adversaries.
“Mr. President, you’ve been very clear you don’t want adversaries to come too close. I fully agree. And with this deal, they are not,” she said. “We are making sure that they will not be allowed to get any control or significant influence in Greenland.”
Wilner reported from New York and Ceballos from Washington.

articles.title_orig: China to cut tariffs on US farm goods, but list excludes soybeans
articles.title_zh: China to cut tariffs on US farm goods, but list excludes soybeans
articles.content_orig:
BEIJING — The U.S. and China are planning to reduce tariffs on $30 billion worth of goods from each country, according to government announcements from both sides Monday.
The detailed lists includes mostly imports of toys, sports equipment and Christmas decorations by the U.S., while American agricultural products accounted for much of the far longer list of imports by China.
Washington has sought to reduce its record trade deficit with Beijing, as the Asian country exports far more to the U.S. than it imports. U.S. goods trade deficit with China was more than $202 billion last year.
"If we see the tariff cuts actually implemented before the holiday season, it could provide a welcome boost to U.S. consumption and to retailers," said Jacob Cooke, CEO at WPIC.
Cooke, whose company primarily helps U.S. brands sell in China, said that Beijing's import list includes fast-growing categories such as hair care and packaged pet food, where Chinese brands are highly competitive against U.S. offerings. "Every percentage point counts for price competitiveness and preserving margin."
However, it was not immediately clear when lower tariffs would take effect, and by how much the duties would go down. The U.S. and China last year slapped import tariffs effectively of over 40% and more than 30%, respectively, on each other.
The two countries limited further tariff increases after a one-year truce reached last fall. Last week, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said negotiators agreed to extend that truce to January.
Monday's announcement followed U.S. President Donald Trump's summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington, D.C., last week. The two sides said the highly anticipated U.S.-China "Board of Trade" would consist of officials from both governments, and would meet at least once a quarter , with the top officials meeting "whenever necessary."
Lower tariffs could substantially boost trade, especially for highly competitive Chinese companies. Home goods seller Ryan Zhao, director of Jiangsu Green Willow Textile, expects sales in the second half of the year to grow by 30% from a year ago if tariff cuts are implemented.
Here's a select list of products set to benefit:
Plates, cups, bowls, serving dishes
Blankets (including electric ones) and rugs
Christmas-tree lamps and ornaments
Toys (including tricycles, but excluding items that connect to WiFi or Bluetooth)
Billiards balls, chalk and tables
Rackets for games, other than for "lawn-tennis or badminton"
Soccer balls, baseballs, softballs, lawn-tennis balls
Fish hooks and fishing line
Horses, donkeys, cattle, pigs, sheep, goats, chickens for breeding
Frozen, fresh or chilled whole chickens or turkeys
Rabbit meat, excluding rabbit heads
Dried, smoked or salted beef
Live freshwater ornamental fish
Ice cream and other frozen products
—CNBC's Matthew Tan contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: ‘Storm fatigue’: Hawaiians reeling from back-to-back hurricanes as Nolo’s threats diminish
articles.title_zh: ‘Storm fatigue’: Hawaiians reeling from back-to-back hurricanes as Nolo’s threats diminish
articles.content_orig:
HILO, Hawaii — Hawaiians have storm fatigue , Hilo’s mayor said Sunday, as the third hurricane to approach the islands in recent weeks continues to spin offshore.
The relatively calm state has been battered by the effects of multiple hurricanes, including Lala, Lowell and now Nolo, as the eastern and central Pacific have churned out at least 19 named storms. None of the three hurricanes has made landfall in Hawaii.
“So there’s storm fatigue and there’s some PTSD,” Mayor Kimo Alameda told NBC News on Sunday.
“I mean, you know, there’s a lot of anxiety around the weather now. You know, a lot of our folks out in the south side, they experienced, you know, catastrophic flooding,” he said, referring to the impacts of Hurricane Lala last month.
That storm killed two people, Alameda said, and damaged more than 200 homes without making landfall. Gov. Josh Green subsequently issued three disaster proclamations related to damage from separate storms in September alone.
Hurricane Nolo brings heavy rain as it skirts Hawaii
Officials have reported some rescues but no deaths or major damage from Nolo.
“We did take some hits in some parts of the island,” Alameda said. “For the most part, we dodged a huge bullet. It could have been much worse.”
More than 120 National Guard members were activated on the island for Nolo, among roughly 400 statewide, after Green issued an emergency proclamation. President Donald Trump recently approved an emergency declaration, authorizing the Federal Emergency Management Agency to coordinate assistance and provide funding support.
In Nāʻālehu, at the island’s southern point, Peggy McKibbin surveyed silt-covered roads from her four-wheeler Sunday and pointed out the lingering damage from Lala — a bakery, a fire station and a hardware store wiped out.
“Everyone has been very much affected by this,” McKibbin said.
Nolo was a Category 4 major hurricane Sunday afternoon and forecast to strengthen, but the center was expected to remain south and southwest of the Hawaiian Islands.
A hurricane watch was in effect for the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument, which the storm was expected to approach Tuesday, according to the National Hurricane Center.
The Pacific has been unusually active this season , according to National Weather Service lead forecaster Bob Oravec, with storm activity running above average during what is already the peak of hurricane season. He said the pattern is consistent with El Niño years, when the Pacific often gets more tropical storms and hurricanes.
Alameda, Hilo’s mayor, said people are ready if another hurricane comes their way.
“Unfortunately, we’ve been having a lot of practice,” he said, noting a recent tsunami threat and earthquake, as well as a precautionary eye on the volcano Kīlauea .
Mexico’s Baja Peninsula, meanwhile, was bracing for the arrival of major Hurricane Polo on Monday after it lashed parts of the country’s southwest coast with rain and strong winds. Polo remained a dangerous Category 3 storm with top sustained winds of 125 mph, the U.S. National Hurricane Center in Miami said Sunday afternoon.
Polo was moving to the north-northwest at 12 mph about 285 miles west-southwest of Cabo San Lucas at the peninsula’s southern tip, according to the hurricane center.
The Mexican navy said in a statement that it had gathered personnel and humanitarian aid in the ports of Guaymas and Mazatlán, on the Pacific Coast, and deployed three vessels that could ship aid to coastal communities isolated by the hurricane.
Also Sunday, Tropical Storm Rachel formed off Mexico’s southwest coast. Rachel had maximum sustained winds of 40 mph and was about 275 miles south of Acapulco. A tropical storm watch was in effect.

articles.title_zh: SpaceX’s Starship Is Set to Make Its First Orbital Flight
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX plans to launch its massive Starship rocket early Monday in an effort to reach orbit with the spacecraft for the first time.
According to SpaceX's website , the 75-minute launch window begins at 8:15 a.m. ET, or 7:15 a.m. local time, from the company town of Starbase, Texas.
The Federal Aviation Administration told CNBC by email that it issued a "license authorization for the SpaceX Starship Super Heavy Flight 14 launch and reentry operations" on Sept. 26. With the 14th test flight of Starship, Elon Musk's aerospace and defense company also plans to deploy 26 of its new Starlink V3 satellites.
Starship is critical to SpaceX's expansion plans. The company is counting on the giant rocket to scale its Starlink , or Connectivity, business, which was its largest and only profitable segment as of the second quarter. SpaceX operates around 11,000 active satellites in orbit today, compared to roughly 650 for competitor Eutelsat OneWeb.
On SpaceX's earnings call in August, Musk said, "It's not out of the question that at some point, Starlink will deliver a majority of the world's internet, at least in countries where we're allowed to operate, which is the vast majority of countries."
SpaceX went public in June in the largest IPO on record and is now valued at about $2 trillion.
SpaceX has designed its Starship Super Heavy rocket and booster to be fully reusable, and to lift more cargo for less cost into orbit than any prior spacecraft. None of the 13 earlier test flights have been intended to make it into orbit, but with the 14th flight, SpaceX is hoping Starship will circle the planet.
The company is preparing Starship for a major NASA test flight next year, and intends to use the rocket to bring U.S. astronauts back to the moon's surface.
SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell said during the All-In Summit earlier this month that the company also plans to use Starship to put "supercompute in space," launching "AI compute satellites" into orbit in 2027.
The company's new v3 satellites , which are produced at a SpaceX facility in Redmond, Washington, are equipped with solar arrays that generate twice as much power as prior generations. They are also larger, and designed to be more powerful, transmitting data more rapidly than earlier versions to Starlink subscribers.

In late summer, when almond husks split open, workers at Creekside Farming in Madera gear up machinery to shake the trees. Tractors zoom around, fallen nuts are collected, and trucks cart off the bins of almonds.
The whole process relies on diesel fuel, which has grown extremely expensive in recent months, said farm owner Jay Mahil, whose family has been growing wine grapes, citrus and other crops in the Central Valley for four generations.
The national average price of diesel hit a new record high of $5.85 per gallon Friday, while California’s average climbed to about $7.71, according to the AAA motor club.
The oil product undergirds much of the global economy, and California, a major player, is no exception to the pain caused by ongoing supply chain disruptions stemming from the U.S.  war with Iran.
The higher fuel costs are squeezing businesses across various industries in California, which has massive trucking and agricultural sectors that rely heavily on diesel to power equipment.
Mahil said his fuel costs are up 40% from this time last year.
“These higher costs come at the worst time for us, “ Mahil said. “These are highly inundated time frames.”
Mahil keeps a close eye on prices. When there’s an occasional slump or dip in the oil market, he orders several truckloads of fuel. But other businesses usually have the same idea, and the fuel depots often run out those days.
“We are running a little leaner right now, with less oil in the tanks,” Mahil said.
California diesel prices set a  record earlier on in the war, at around $7.75 per gallon in April.
Greg Dubuque, general manager for a trucking fleet based out of Montebello, noted that the cost to fill his trucks in California has gone from around $1,200 in April to $1,800.
“It’s a dramatic impact, especially for us smaller companies,” he said.
Gene Seroka, executive director of the Port of Los Angeles, said more than two-thirds of cargo moving in and out of the port is carried by trucks. And of the some 1,200 trucking companies that do business at the port, more than 50% are small to medium-sized companies that are seriously struggling with prices, Seroka said.
“It’s difficult for companies to absorb such an energy shock as we’ve seen over the past six months,” Seroka said.
The turmoil in the Persian Gulf region is forcing cargo away from the Suez Canal and onto a longer route around the southern tip of Africa, creating longer transit times that burn more fuel and drive costs up further, Seroka said.
Increased diesel prices are  pushing up the cost to transport food. Frozen and refrigerated goods, such as fresh produce, are most sensitive to price increases because diesel is typically used to power both cold storage and transportation.
Nick Vyas, a supply chain expert and professor at USC Marshall School of Business, said that while companies try to absorb some of the cost increase, grocery prices are starting to tick up in stores.
Though grocery costs may decrease slightly once fuel costs stabilize, they are unlikely to return to  prewar baselines as retailers adjust to higher prices, Vyas noted, pointing to sustained increases in food costs post-pandemic.
With American refiners funneling the fuel oil into international markets, the domestic supply has dwindled, driving up prices. Diesel prices jumped 7 cents overnight, 24 cents in the past week, 48 cents in the past month and $2.14 compared with this time last year, according to AAA.
Kandace Redd, a AAA spokesperson, said the organization’s past research shows that consumers are most likely to drive less, combine errands and reduce shopping or dining out to cope with record pump prices.
Diesel prices in California are typically above the national average as the state faces cost pressures from higher taxes and environmental standards, Vyas said. Because around 40% of goods imported in the U.S. pass through the San Pedro and Long Beach ports, California’s energy costs also expose the rest of the nation’s supply chain to these increases.
Larger companies are better poised to absorb some of the shock of increased prices through higher profit margins and the ability to buy in bulk, Vyas said. Mom-and-pop businesses, such as small trucking fleets or family farms, are hit harder.
“When you’re a large national truckload carrier, the J.B. Hunts and the Swifts and the Werners of the world, they do a lot of hedging on fuel,” meaning they establish advance agreements to purchase fuel at a fixed cost, Dubuque said.
His smaller fleet of 40 trucks, on the other hand, is generally stuck paying the price at the pump.
Dubuque is taking several steps to try and mitigate the impact. This includes explaining the rising cost of doing business to his customers, avoiding refueling in California where possible and using alternative fuels to power air conditioning in trucks overnight.
But as the manager of a smaller company, he is nervous about how long these strategies will work if diesel prices don’t start dipping.
A similar disparity is seen when it comes to the impact of rising diesel prices on consumers, Vyas noted. For low-income households, any uptick in grocery prices will stretch already strained budgets, while wealthier consumers may not notice the change.
Economist Christopher Thornberg has a more optimistic outlook on the impact of rising fuel prices on the average consumer. He pointed out that fuel prices have been notably low in recent years. He said the current diesel spike is not exceptionally high when put in the context of inflation-adjusted averages over the last two decades.
“Sure, it’s a shock from where it was six months ago, but from a long-run perspective, once you control for price growth, it’s not a big deal,”  said Thornberg, founding partner of Beacon Economics.
Inflation-adjusted diesel prices have reached higher than the current $5.85 national average per gallon. The 2008 peak of $4.74 a gallon is equivalent to $7.20 in today’s dollars, while the more recent 2022 peak of almost $5.82 would be about $6.56 today.
And while certain industries  such as trucking remain reliant on diesel fuel, alternative energy sources and increased domestic oil production have made the American economy as a whole less sensitive to fluctuations in global fuel prices compared  with past energy crises, he noted.
Nonetheless, news of a  record high in national diesel prices is likely to disturb consumers and carry political ramifications for the  Trump administration, Thornberg said.
AP-NORC polling shows that around two-thirds of Americans disapprove of  the president’s handling of the economy. The continued surge in diesel and oil prices is unwelcome news for the Republican Party heading into November’s midterm elections.

articles.title_zh: AEW star Pac mourned fellow wrestler Andy Williams in heartbreaking final post — week before own death at 40
articles.content_orig:
Pro-wrestling star Benjamin Satterley, known as Pac in All Elite Wrestling, mourned his late peer Andy Williams in a heartbreaking tribute — just 10 days before his own death .
On Sept. 17, Satterley shared a lighthearted throwback photo alongside Williams, who had died two weeks earlier after suffering a medical episode during a tag-team match.
Satterley and Williams — wearing matching flame-printed bandanas — flexed and smirked as they posed backstage at an undisclosed wrestling event.
“We always knew you were an anomaly too good for this world,” Satterley said in a televised tribute for Williams on Sept. 12 . “I just want to say I love you, man. And you always made sure that I knew you loved me too. I’ll miss you, my friend. ‘Till we meet again.”
The high-flying Satterley died at the age of 40, All Elite Wrestling announced on Sunday night.
No cause of death was given.
Satterley, who signed with the Jacksonville-based wrestling company in 2019, competed at AEW’s pay-per-view event “All Out” at NOW Arena in Chicago on Saturday night.
He notably was AEW’s inaugural All-Atlantic champion and a two-time World Trios champion.
“Benjamin Satterley defined excellence, as a beloved husband & friend to his many loved ones, + in his wrestling knowledge, skill, unprecedented athleticism, professionalism, consistency + dedication to the sport that he loved & traveled the world to pursue,” said Tony Khan, AEW’s owner and chief operating officer .
He also starred in WWE from 2012 to 2018 as “Neville,” where he held the WWE Cruiserweight Championship, the NXT Championship and NXT Tag Team Championship.
Satterley’s death comes on the same day in which Williams’ family, loved ones and fans gathered for a public celebration of life at Buffalo RiverWorks in Buffalo, NY.
Williams, 48, was competing in a tag team match with partner Jesse “The Blade” Guilmette at Mr. Small’s Theatre in Millvale, Pa., when he knocked his head against the ringpost and later collapsed.
Williams, known to wrestling fans as “The Butcher” and guitarist for “Every Time I Die,” was given CPR before he was rushed to Allegheny General Hospital, where he was pronounced dead, according to Love Wrestling, which organized the event.
The Allegheny County Medical Examiner’s Office confirmed Williams died following a medical crisis, but no preliminary cause of death was stated.
“Anybody who knew Andy, they were his friend,” Williams’ father, Frank, told WIVB on Sunday. “If he had a dollar in his pocket and you needed it, he would try to get you a dollar and a quarter. He was that type of guy where money meant nothing to him, friendship meant everything, and that was my son.”

Fund managers warn investors of losses as some US-focused products trade well above asset values
Several Chinese mutual funds investing in US stocks have warned investors about risks associated with hefty premiums to their net asset values, highlighting persistent demand for US equities even after Beijing expanded quotas for outbound investment.
At least six fund houses, including China Asset Management, Hua An Fund Management and China Universal Asset Management, issued warnings after the market prices of some of their funds rose substantially above their net asset values, cautioning that investors who chase the rally could incur losses if the premiums narrow.
Much like the price-to-book value for stocks of listed companies, a fund’s premium to net asset value measures how much fund prices outpace real values. A big aberration could imply a pullback ahead that would send prices down to reasonable levels.

After the Kansas City Chiefs defeated the Miami Dolphins 24-10, they are 3-0 on the season. While Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce only made two catches during the game — he made the most of them.
Kelce caught a 48-yard pass from Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes on the very first snap. During the fourth quarter, Mahomes connected with Kelce on an 11-yard touchdown pass on third-and-6, giving Kansas a 14-point lead with 2:55 left in regulation.
"All of a sudden Travis is right there behind everybody," Mahomes told reporters after the game. "When you have a big tight end like that, he can make a big play and go up and get it. Big play, big-time play for a big-time player, and helped win us the game."
Kelce's wife, Taylor Swift, did not attend the Chiefs' Week 3 matchup at Hard Rock Stadium. Swift was in Los Angeles for the 2026 Video Music Awards. While Kelce could not join Swift at the Peacock Theatre on September 27, he made sure to support her from afar.
GettyTaylor Swift walks the teal carpet at the 2026 Video Music Awards in Los Angeles.
During the Chiefs' flight back to Kansas City, Kelce was on his phone hitting like on several posts shared by Billboard featuring Swift on Instagram. One caption read , "The Showgirl herself has arrived to the 2026 #VMAs ❤️‍🔥," the other simply read, "Taylor Swift arrives at the 2026."
Swift looked gorgeous in a Tamara Ralph couture dress with Le Silla metallic silver sandals.
He also liked Good Morning America's post that shared a video of the pop star on the teal carpet. They wrote, "The queen has arrived! Taylor Swift glides down the #vmas carpet where she's receiving the inaugural MTV VMA Artist Director Honors."
Swift will receive the VMAs' first-ever Artist Director Honors on Sunday night, making her the most-awarded artist in VMA history.
The award goes to artists "whose work behind the camera has expanded the possibilities of music video and advanced the art of visual storytelling," and "celebrates a sustained and influential body of work from artists who have pushed creative boundaries and developed a clear directorial voice."
Two days before the Chiefs-Dolphins game, Swift dropped new music for the first time since marrying Kelce, a four-song EP, "The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore." Included in the mix, " Cleveland! " a beloved tribute to the 11-time Pro Bowler and his hometown.
However, the EP's first single is "Patient Zero." During the VMAs, Swift will premiere the star-studded music video featuring herself, Dakota Johnson, and Colin Farrell.
Swift previously took home the directing award at the VMAs for "The Man," "All Too Well: The Short Film," "Anti-Hero," and "Fortnight."

In his first Labour Party conference speech as Chancellor, John Healey said the government plans to bring back hope through a "new age of industrialisation", announcing new funding for shipbuilding and manufacturing.
Also addressing the conference this morning were Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, here's what we heard:

Dharshini David Deputy economics editor
The Chancellorâs speech leant heavily on the concept of hope, but at its heart was a dose of financial reality.
Whatever the governmentâs spending ambitions,
the indication was  the forthcoming Budget would be about fiscal
discipline, rather than extra cash.
We do, after all, spend more on interest
payments on existing public debt than any government department, apart from
health.
But there remains many questions about how the Chancellor
will realise goals such as faster growth and better employment opportunities.
The extra funds for apprenticeships will, for example, be a welcome boost â but
itâs a relatively small one â and many sectors continue to grapple with higher
costs of employing staff, including tax changes imposed by the previous
Chancellor.
So, there is much yet to be resolved â and while optimism is
crucial for a thriving economy, hope alone wonât do the job.
The reinstatement of the Union Learning Fund , a trade union-run programme to provide workers with extra education, also featured in John Healey's speech.
The chancellor said 180,000 workers had received new training each year
through the fund before it was abolished by the Tories in 2021.
Set up in 1998, the aim of the fund has been to help support the most disadvantaged learners in the labour market, focusing on maths and English, and the take-up of high quality apprenticeships.
Employees did not need to be union members to take part in the scheme.
It also focused on digital skills and training for jobs in growing industries, such as advanced manufacturing.
Before it was closed in 2021, the fund was managed and
administered by Unionlearn, an organisation run by the Trades Union Congress.
Chancellor John Healey criticised the economic record of the previous Conservative governments , telling his partyâs conference they âleft Britain spending more on debt than the Home Office, defence and justice put togetherâ.
Back in March, the Office for Budget Responsibly (OBR) - the official spending watchdog - forecast debt interest would cost Â£135bn in 2026-27.
Thatâs higher than the Home Office, Justice and Defence budgets, which are expected to total Â£103bn this year.
The OBR is due to update the official debt interest forecast at next monthâs Budget.
Itâs important to note that debt interest costs have continued to rise under the Labour government. At the start of this month, long-term market borrowing costs climbed to their highest levels since 1998.
Former Labour minister Alan Milburn is producing a final report on youth unemployment
In his speech, the chancellor referred to Alan Milburn's upcoming report into youth unemployment , describing how the Labour minister's ongoing work "lays bare the scale" of the challenges young people face.
This is has been a key focus of Labour since its general election win in 2024, with former PM Keir Starmer describing Milburn's interim report in May as "sobering".
The latest official figures, released last month , suggest 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 were not in education, employment or training (Neet) between April and June 2026 - a 3% increase on the same time last year.
Reacting to these latest figures, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said the government was determined to "turn the tide" on the youth unemployment crisis.
The final instalment of Milburn's report - including recommendations for how to tackle the problems outlined - is expected to be published later this year.
Jennifer McKiernan Reporting from Liverpool
There was clearly a lot of support for John Healey in his first conference speech as chancellor, as he outlined how getting young people into work was key to his vision ahead of his first Budget on 28 October.
As a veteran Labour politician, Healey sprinkled his speech with anecdotes about his time in government that kept delegates laughing, including his tale of lending Gordon Brown his red tie at the 1999 Labour conference.
Notably, some of the biggest cheers were for the re-establishment of the Union Learning Fund - a fund relatively unknown outside the trade union circles who are at the conference in force.
Healey was careful not to say too much about his Budget plans, though offered new announcements about Rolls-Royce factories and Royal Navy floating docks that went down a storm with the party faithful.

This speech had a distinct defence flavour
to it, but big questions remain on that area for the chancellor.
Healey resigned as defence secretary, a move that many
saw as one of the final nails in the coffin for Keir Starmerâs premiership.
He announced Â£6bn of new contracts for British shipyards ,
which he said would help defend the UK for decades to come.
But the chancellor still needs to find almost Â£5bn in
next monthâs Budget to fund the Defence Investment Plan.
And he's under pressure to set out when and how the UK
will reach 3% of GDP on defence spending.
Expect that to be one of the biggest talking points
around Healey in the coming weeks and months.
Healey says "national industrial strength is national security" as he announces the government will commit Â£6bn of contracts for British shipyards.
Funding will be used to build new docks for new submarines, which Healey says will be built "in Britain, by British workers" and "will defend us all for decades to come".
The chancellor says British trade unions are "full partners in this new age of industrialisation" as he announces the "rebirth" of the Union Learning Fund.
He says 180,000 workers got new training each year through the fund before it was abolished by the Tories, adding that he's proud to reinstate the fund.

He describes AI as "the greatest innovation of our time" which will "transform our society at every level", adding that the UK will also need to "face the serious risks" it poses to national security.
Returning to his analogy about the miners' lamp , Healey says the government "needs to light the way for a new generation" before finishing his speech.

U.S. President Donald Trump announced over the weekend that he is still looking "very seriously" at implementing a U.S. ban on diesel exports to combat high prices, a move analysts have warned would just fan the flames of the global energy shortage.
Republicans are under pressure to ease high diesel prices for farmers ahead of the midterm elections after a run-up that has pushed the fuel to historic highs.
Most analysts agree a ban on exports would be at best self-defeating.
Resource researcher Wood Mackenzie warns that not only would a U.S. ban draw down diesel stocks worldwide, it would also force U.S. refineries to cut production and raise gas prices.
Its analysis estimates that a ban on exports would fill storage in the United States within weeks and force producers to cut the volume of oil going to refineries.
"The irony of a U.S. diesel export ban is that it would likely increase costs for American consumers," said Alan Gelder, a commodities researcher at Wood Mackenzie.
"Cutting crude runs to manage the oversupply would shift the cost burden from diesel to gasoline, meaning a policy designed to bring relief at the diesel pump could end up driving prices higher at the gasoline pump."
U.S. diesel exports to other countries, especially Europe, have risen in the past six months as the Iran war cut off Middle East supplies and Russia initiated its own export ban to cope with domestic shortages.
A U.S. ban would accelerate stock drawdowns across global markets at a time when Europe's share of U.S. diesel exports is almost 50 per cent, up from 30 per cent last year.
"A ban on U.S. diesel exports would increase competition for non-U.S. barrels in an already tightly supplied market," said Gelder.
"China is currently the only country with material spare refining capacity that could cover the loss of U.S. refinery throughputs. However, China may well decide it is not in its interest to do this."
David Oxley, chief climate and commodities economist at Capital Economics, said the scale of the economic shock that could stem from a complete ban on U.S. diesel exports would be comparable to the natural gas crisis in Europe in 2022.
Natural gas prices in the eurozone then averaged about US$240 a barrel, peaking at more than US$400 per barrel in August of 2022.
Capital Economics believes that some form of export restriction is likely to be announced in coming weeks, as politicians will want to be seen doing something on fuel prices before the midterms.
"This would further complicate the outlooks for energy markets and fuel price inflation," said Oxley.
On the bright side, since a ban won't solve anything and could make things worse, "we suspect that it would be short-lived."

BMO chief economist Douglas Porter said growing concern about government debt is one factor and the higher yields go, the bigger interest payments on that debt get.
Canada's interest payment to revenue ratio peaked above 35 per cent in the 1990s, triggering austerity measures. By the early 2020s it was down to 6 per cent, but since the pandemic it has risen to almost 11 per cent.
That is still better than south of the border. In the United States federal debt interest has climbed to the post-war high of almost 20 per cent of revenues.
"Given still-rising debt loads and that maturing debt is rolling off into higher rates, this ratio is poised to push even higher in coming years — possibly above 25 per cent in 10 years," said Porter in a note.

Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses the miracles of Lourdes, Pope Leo XIV's expected visit there, and kratom as authorities await the toxicology reports in the deaths of two Ole Miss students on 'America Reports.'
Pope Leo XIV arrived in Lourdes from Paris on Saturday evening for his first-ever visit to the renowned place of miracle cures.
Back in 1858, a 14-year-old peasant girl named Bernadette Soubirous reported having 18 visions of the Virgin Mary at the Lourdes Massabielle Grotto. This ultimately led to her being named a saint.
The pope prayed at the Grotto Saturday night before leading an open-air Mass on the Prairie on Sunday, with hundreds of thousands expected to be in attendance.

He also planned to meet with bishops, the sick and the support staff.
I spoke with Dr. Alessandro de Franciscis, who recently retired as president of the Lourdes Office of Medical Observation after 17 years of reviewing treatments and possible miracle cures.
Pope Leo XIV presides over Mass at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026, in Lourdes, France. (AP Images)
He discussed his upcoming meeting with the pope, who he said was visiting Lourdes in the name of purification and healing, including healing from the Church's recent sexual abuse scandals.

"I think I love him," he told me. "I think he's doing very well (as pope). He's talking of the challenges that we have. You must have heard about his first encyclical letter on artificial intelligence ... all the good that this technology can bring to today's world. He's a guy from Chicago. I love him. We all love him!"
Priests sit before a Mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, France, on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. (AP Images)
Dr. de Franciscis said the pope would meet with people whose miracle healings were investigated and later recognized by the Church.
Those include Sister Bernadette Moriau, who was cured of a spinal condition and was able to walk again, and Antonietta Raco, who in 2009 was cured of the severe neurodegenerative disease primary lateral sclerosis.

But for Lourdes, as well as for the pope, spiritual and physical healing lead to both minor and major miracles, according to de Franciscis.

"These so-called spiritual cures are so, so much more numerous than the physical ones that we know."
"I think that statistically, these so-called spiritual cures are so, so much more numerous than the physical ones that we know," he said to me from Lourdes, as he eagerly anticipated the pope’s visit.
